entry.title: asr: give RoutedASR/Refiner a close() so pytest no longer leaks 19GB …
entry.content:
asr: give RoutedASR/Refiner a close() so pytest no longer leaks 19GB (#55)

* asr: give RoutedASR, Refiner and TranslationWorker a close()

Each of these classes started a daemon thread that looped forever on a
queue get (Refiner, TranslationWorker) or ran an untracked preload
(RoutedASR), with no way to stop it. The thread's frame holds its owner,
and a Refiner holds the RoutedASR, which holds the sherpa-onnx
recognizers -- so an engine could never be collected once built.

close() on each: FIFO stop sentinel + thread join for the two queue
workers (so already-queued work still runs first), and for RoutedASR a
tracked-thread join followed by dropping the recognizers, punct,
ko_spacer, LID and segmentation VAD. Work submitted after close raises
(Refiner: dropping refine text would lose transcript content, and a
force_sync refine would otherwise deadlock) or is dropped
(TranslationWorker: the line was already printed untranslated).
main()'s shutdown path closes all three.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* tests: guard the pipeline lifecycle against the 19GB pytest leak

Model-free stubs cover the mechanism itself (a closed Refiner releases
its engine; a closed RoutedASR joins its preload thread, drops every
model reference and becomes collectable; both refuse work afterwards),
so CI without models/ still catches a regression. One models-gated test
runs the real make_ja_golden.run_clip() twice and asserts no RoutedASR
survives it -- that loop is where the 19GB came from.

Thread leaks are checked by comparing threading.enumerate() before and
after each test rather than by name: threading.Thread(target=...) names
its threads "Thread-N", so there is no _worker_loop/_preload_rest to
match on.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* tests: teach the RoutedASR/Refiner stubs about the closed state

transcribe(), partial(), identify() and add_span() now check that their
object is still open, and these stubs call those methods unbound, so
they need the same state. Borrowed from the real classes rather than
faked, matching how the stubs already borrow _looks_truncated and
add_span.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs: document the pipeline shutdown path in the embedding guide

An embedding app is exactly the caller that hits this: stopping
run_stream releases nothing, and a dropped-but-unclosed pipeline keeps
its recognizers resident for the life of the process. Says which order
to close in, that close() ends the object's life rather than pausing it,
and points at reset_live_session() for the "new conversation, same
models" case.

asr: survive a missing omni fallback model; download the int8 omnilingual tarball (#51)

* asr: keep the live process alive when the omni fallback model is missing

Problem: transcribe()'s empty-specialist safety net called _get("omni")
without catching ModelUnavailable. On an install without the omnilingual
model, the first specialist decode that came back empty raised out of
run_stream() and took the whole live process (mic, --serve dashboard,
runtime API) down mid-stream. Seen 2026-09-04 while testing language
switching: a short English "Once." under a ja tag was enough.

Change: catch ModelUnavailable there, like every other _get() caller
already does, and let the empty result stand (the caller drops empty
finals as non-speech).

Effect: a minimal install degrades to "no fallback" instead of dying.
Two stub-based tests cover both branches.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* download_models: fetch the int8 omnilingual tarball and refuse partial dirs

Problem: the omnilingual entry pointed at the fp32 tarball
(...300M-ctc-2025-11-12) while asking for model.int8.onnx, which that
tarball does not contain (it ships model.onnx only). The selective
extractor kept whatever matched, so the model directory ended up holding
only tokens.txt, and because "present" was tested on the directory rather
than its files, every later run skipped it as complete. The live fallback
route therefore had no model to load.

Change: point at the upstream int8 tarball
(...300M-ctc-int8-2025-11-12, model.int8.onnx 365,352,120 bytes, the
same artifact the 2026-08-24 benchmarks used); treat "present" as "every
wanted file exists" so a partial directory is re-fetched; and raise (after
removing the partial directory) when a tarball lacks a wanted file.

Effect: a fresh download restores the fallback model; the stale layout
repairs itself on the next run. Three tests exercise the extractor with
tiny synthetic tarballs.

entry.content:
eval: ReazonSpeech head dropout on FLEURS ja: pre-roll vs silence prepend, greedy vs beam (#46)

* eval: measure ReazonSpeech head dropout under 8 onset x decoder conditions

scripts/eval_head_dropout.py runs the live path's VAD verbatim
(realtime_transcribe.build_vad defaults, 512-sample windows, flush at end),
picks the first utterance-bearing segment of each clip, and decodes it under
greedy_search/modified_beam_search x {none, preroll, silence300,
silence1000}, plus a RoutedASR(forced_lang="ja") reference row.

The raw grid builds its own recognizers with _build_reazon's exact
configuration, varying only decoding_method, so split-retry and LID cannot
interfere with what is being measured. Scoring reuses
eval_accuracy.normalize_ja plus a character alignment whose reference side is
end-free, because the hypothesis covers one segment while the FLEURS
reference covers the whole clip.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs: head dropout measured on FLEURS ja, pre-roll vs silence prepend

FLEURS ja 100 clips, first utterance-bearing VAD segment, Ryzen 5 5600,
--threads 4, sherpa-onnx 1.13.6. On the onset-resolvable subset (n=90): no
onset handling drops the utterance head in 27/90 decodes with beam and 29/90
with greedy -- the decoding method does not protect the head. Pre-roll takes
that to 0/90 (mean CER 0.188 -> 0.086) for +10% decode time; prepending 300ms
of silence takes it to 4/90 and 1.0s to 2/90, so silence is a workable but
weaker substitute for an implementation that keeps no pre-onset audio.
split-retry never fired (0/100): a 2-5 character head loss does not move text
density enough to trip its gate, so it is not the first line of defence.

elsewhere, and scripts/dump_ja_config.py has to be able to report that

Hoisted, not changed: RZ_MODEL_TYPE / RZ_DECODING_METHOD / RZ_MODELING_UNIT /
RZ_HOTWORDS_SCORE / RZ_MODEL_FILES out of _build_reazon(), VAD_MIN_SPEECH_S /
VAD_BUFFER_S / VAD_NUM_THREADS out of build_vad(), and PUNCT_* out of
PunctuatorJa.__init__'s signature. Every value is identical.

punct_ja.py additionally moves numpy / onnxruntime / fugashi into the methods
that use them, so `import punct_ja` for the constants alone costs nothing.
CI installs none of the three, and the punctuation model is an optional
363 MB download. Constructing a PunctuatorJa still raises the same
ImportError for a missing fugashi that importing the module used to raise.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs: specify the Japanese route for re-implementation

Another project is rebuilding this pipeline in C++ (a Godot GDExtension over
sherpa-onnx's distributed binaries, running the punctuation model through the
ONNX Runtime sherpa-onnx already bundles). Everything it needs was spread
across asr_engine.py, realtime_transcribe.py, punct_ja.py, PUNCT_JA.md,
MOBILE.md and BENCHMARKS.md, and some of it only existed as a literal in a
function.

docs/JA_PIPELINE.md (Japanese) collects it: model list with sha256 and
licenses, every OfflineRecognizerConfig value including the feature settings
that are sherpa defaults, the VAD settings with the measurements behind them,
the head-dropout phenomenon and all three countermeasures with their exact
constants, the call order from VAD to final text with which stages are
optional, and a complete C++ reproduction spec for the punctuation restorer
(I/O, vocab, MeCab-free tokenization with the evidence counts, thresholds,
post-processing order, question suffixes, the `？` -> `?。` quirk, the ORT
call sequence, and what is verified on which platform).

Two things a re-implementation would otherwise get wrong are called out: the
upstream punct_bert.int8.onnx is non-functional and must not be used, and
hotwords cannot be encoded against this recognizer's byte-level BPE tokens.

The numbers come from scripts/dump_ja_config.py, which reports the effective
ja configuration as JSON without loading a model, and are committed as
docs/ja_pipeline_spec.json. tests/test_ja_pipeline_spec.py re-runs the dump
and compares, so the document drifting from the code is a failing test. The
model half of that comparison only runs where models/ is populated.

* test: pin the ja route's output on eight FLEURS clips

directory's README and in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md) and golden.json: the exact
finals and refine text the pipeline emits for each, plus the CER against the
FLEURS reference for transparency and the machine the run was recorded on.

scripts/make_ja_golden.py regenerates it by running the pipeline, not a
re-creation of it: the same objects main() builds for `--wav X --no-realtime
--mode single --lang ja --threads 4`, with results read off the EventHub via
add_listener rather than scraped from stdout. Two full regenerations produced
identical output on this machine, and the test's own run made a third.

The clips were chosen to cover 6.5-12.5 s, to exercise the CJK ITN pass
(ja_085 and ja_090: 千九百四十年八月十五日 -> 1940年八月15日, 三十四件 -> 34件),
and to pin one real failure on purpose (ja_044 loses its first sentence to
head dropout). No FLEURS ja reference contains a question mark at all, so the
punctuator's `？` rule is not covered here; the Dart parity fixture covers it
with synthetic cases.

tests/test_ja_golden.py compares at two levels: exact match is reported, and
the pass condition is CER against the golden text at most 1.0% per clip,
because int8 ONNX kernels are not bit-reproducible across CPU
microarchitectures. At these clip lengths 1.0% admits zero differing
characters, so today that gate is the same test as exact match -- the README
says so plainly and the test also prints a set-level CER for diagnosis. Skips
without models/ or testdata/.

* docs: fold the measured head-dropout rates into JA_PIPELINE

The placeholder table is replaced with the numbers from
docs/HEAD_DROPOUT.md (merged separately), stated with the conditions they
were measured under: FLEURS ja test split 100 clips (read speech, CC BY 4.0),
one VAD segment per clip (the first at least 1.0 s long), Silero at
threshold 0.5 / min silence 0.35 s / 512-sample windows, Ryzen 5 5600,
4 threads, sherpa-onnx 1.13.6. Both the 90-clip onset-resolvable subset and
the 100-clip totals are given, with the definitions of "head dropout"
(2+ leading reference characters deleted, 60%+ of the hypothesis aligned)
and of the subset (clips where at least one condition reached the
reference's first character) spelled out, since neither number means
anything without them.

The conclusion is written at the strength the measurement supports: real
audio pre-roll is the standard (0/90 with beam), silence prepend is a weaker
but workable alternative for an implementation whose VAD keeps no pre-onset
audio (2-4/90, explicitly not claimed significant at that scale), and
decoding method does not protect the onset at all (greedy 29/90 vs beam
27/90 with no countermeasure). Pre-roll costs about +10% decode time, with a
note that run-to-run noise is the same order so smaller ms differences are
not real. _split_retry fired 0/100 times, so the production row's 0/90 is
pre-roll's alone and split-retry cannot be specified as a head-dropout
countermeasure.

未検証事項 now records what the measurement does not reach (read speech, one
dataset, one machine, first segment only, two prepend lengths) instead of an
unmeasured placeholder.

Also fixes an attribution in the 現象 list. The 資料は -> 昨日は observation
is recorded in three independent places, not one, so all three are cited:
docs/BENCHMARKS.md's 2026-09-01 live-path section (desktop Python),
docs/MOBILE.md's Android emulator run 2, and today's condition grid.

entry.title: hayamimi_core 0.1.0 release prep: punctuation in refine (#15 phase 2)…
entry.content:
<pre style='white-space:pre-wrap;width:81ex'>hayamimi_core 0.1.0 release prep: punctuation in refine (#15 phase 2), pub.dev readiness (#16), emulator-driven fixes (#45)
* live: describe a session's punctuation model in the decode protocol
A refine ("清書") pass sends its audio to the decode worker isolate and gets text back, and neither side had any way to talk about punctuation: the worker could not be told which model to load, and a result could not say whether anything had been restored into it.
DecodeWorkerConfig gains the four things PunctuatorJa.load needs — the model file, its vocabulary, an optional ONNX Runtime library path, and intra-op threads — plus punctuatePlainSession, and DecodeWorkerResult gains punctuated. shouldPunctuateRefine sits beside them as the rule itself: a routed session punctuates what came back as Japanese, a plain session has no language tag to test and goes by the flag. Keeping the rule here, as a pure function of the config and one result's language, is what lets it be read and tested on its own rather than inferred from the worker's decode loop.
JaPunctuation is the caller-facing half: an immutable description of where the two files live, with no imports of its own, so the protocol stays free of FFI and testable without any native library.
Nothing loads or applies a model yet — this is the vocabulary for it, so a session that passes none behaves exactly as before.
Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
* live: load the punctuation model in the decode worker, and use it on refines
Phase 1 of #15 landed PunctuatorJa but left it unwired, so a mobile session's refine ("清書") output was still an unbroken run of characters while the desktop pipeline's read as sentences. This wires it in.
The worker loads it after its recognizers, when the session's config names one, and reports it on the same model_load start/done events every other model uses, as model: 'punct'. It then runs restore() over refine results whose language it applies to, inside the same timed section and the same try as the decode: the reported latency is what the worker actually took, and a restore() that throws loses that one refine and leaves the session running, exactly as a failed decode does.
It lives here, beside the recognizers, because restore() is another synchronous native call — tens of milliseconds per refine on the Windows x86 host the parity test runs on — and running it on the caller's isolate would hand back the pause that moving decoding off it removed.
Only refine results are punctuated. That is where the desktop pipeline punctuates, and it is the pass with the context for it: a final covers one speech segment and a draft part of one still being spoken, so sentence boundaries there fall wherever the speaker paused. Punctuating every final would also add a full model run per utterance, on a phone, for a line the next refine replaces.
A load failure frees whatever was already built and reports a build failure naming the model, so a session never comes up quietly producing unpunctuated text.
loadWorkerPunctuator takes a callback rather than the worker's SendPort so a test can build exactly what a config would build without spawning an isolate — as close to the real worker as a flutter test run can get, since the recognizers beside it need native libraries no test VM can load. The test skips when the 182 MB model or an ONNX Runtime library is absent.
Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
* live: let a session ask for punctuation, and say when it applied
The worker can now punctuate a refine, but nothing could ask it to and nothing downstream could tell it had. This is the caller's half.
start() and startDebugWavStream(), on both LiveTranscriber and the HayamimiLive facade, take an optional JaPunctuation; null keeps today's behaviour. Both files are checked for existence before a worker is spawned, so a missing 182 MB model is reported before up to 396 MB of recognizer weights are loaded for a session that could not have worked. The worker checks again when it loads them — it is the one that can tell a file that exists from a file it can read.
LiveTranscriptEntry and RefineSubtitleEvent gain punctuated (also "punctuated" in toJson, beside every key that was already there), so a consumer can tell text the punctuation model wrote from text the recognizer produced. Only refine entries can carry it.
One ordering detail decides a real case. The refine pass falls back to the fast finals' text when the merged re-decode comes back much shorter than they were, and punctuation is restored in the worker, before that comparison. Restored marks are characters nobody said: one per clause is enough to lift a genuinely truncated re-decode back over the threshold. So the comparison strips them first (withoutRestoredMarks, next to the list of marks the restorer writes) and the fast text it is compared against is left alone, having never been punctuated. When that fallback does fire, the entry reports punctuated: false — the text that survived is the finals', which nothing punctuated.
HayamimiLive.textTransform still runs last, on the punctuated text.
Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
* docs: describe punctuation as a feature you can turn on, not a port
The README's punctuation section still said the model was a port with nothing wired to it, and told a reader to call PunctuatorJa themselves from the textTransform hook. That stopped being true.
It now says how to turn it on (a JaPunctuation on start), what it changes (refine events only, and why), which refines get it in a routed versus a plain session, where it runs and what it costs in memory, that a load failure fails start() rather than degrading quietly, and how the restored marks interact with the refine pass's too-short fallback. The threading table, the events table's refine and model_load rows, and the package layout follow the same change. Using PunctuatorJa directly is still documented, for text the live pipeline did not produce.
Two caveats stay, said plainly: the 182 MB model is still not downloadable, so a host app places it itself, and nothing in this change ran on a device — what a phone's ONNX Runtime does, and what restore() costs on an ARM CPU, is unverified.
The parity test's recorded mean widens from 66–71 ms over three runs to 66–90 ms over six, which is what this host actually produced once the runs from this change are counted.
Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
* docs(hayamimi_core): reach dartdoc 0 warnings, fill consumer-facing doc gaps
dartdoc (the standalone 9.0.9 build, not the SDK's own dartdoc which crashes on Windows independent of this package - dart-lang/dartdoc#4266) reported 11 warnings against this package: five unresolved [Foo] doc references and six broken links from the README (fixed separately). Two of the five were plain mistakes - a doc comment referencing a filename in bracket syntax instead of a code span, in lang_routing.dart and live_transcriber.dart. One was a symbol split across two /// lines ([RoutingProfile\n.jaSenseVoice]), which also wasn't importable from manifest_eval_runner.dart since nothing else in that file uses the type - switched to a code span rather than adding an import dartdoc-only would leave unused.
The remaining two, in draft_pass.dart, were a real bug: isDraftDue's doc comment and slideDraftFrames's doc comment had been concatenated into one block with no blank line between them, so the whole thing attached to slideDraftFrames (the next declaration) and isDraftDue had no doc at all. [isDecoding] and [_runDraftDecode] were both then unresolvable - the former because it isn't slideDraftFrames's parameter, the latter because it's a private member of a different library. Split the comment back onto its two declarations; [isDecoding] now resolves correctly as isDraftDue's own parameter, and [_runDraftDecode] became a code span since it can never resolve (private, cross-library).
Separately, scanned for public API left without any doc comment at all: nine standalone exception/support types (BenchRunException, ModelFileResolutionException, LiveTranscriberException, RemoteEventParseException, RemoteTranscriberException, WavParseException, RoutedRecognizerException, the ModelDownloadProgress typedef, ModelDownloadResponse) and a dozen getters/constructors on the two consumer-facing facades and their transcribers (HayamimiLive.isRunning, HayamimiRemote's constructor and connectionState/state/isConnected, LiveTranscriber.sampleRate/isRunning, RemoteTranscriber's constructor, sampleRate, connectionState/state/isConnected). Left the vendored ONNX Runtime FFI bindings (ort_bindings.dart) and individual self-evident data-class fields undocumented, matching this package's existing convention of documenting a field only when its meaning isn't obvious from the surrounding class doc plus its name.
Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
* chore(hayamimi_core): pubspec metadata for a pub.dev release
pana (pub.dev's scorer) can't run on Windows here to check this directly, so going through its checklist by hand: description was a 286-character multi-line block reusing the package doc's wording - pub.dev wants 60-180 characters, one line for the package listing. Rewrote it to one sentence. Added issue_tracker (homepage/repository were already set) and an explicit platforms: map. The package depends on record and sherpa-onnx's native libraries for android/ios only - without a platforms: map, pub.dev infers support from every transitive dependency's own platforms, which would list web/desktop targets this package has never been run on (see README "Platform status").
Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
* docs(hayamimi_core): rewrite the 0.1.0 changelog as one release entry
The 0.1.0 entry had accumulated bullets from three separate issues (#15, #24, #29) in the order they landed, with the actual "here is what this package is" bullet (on-device transcription, remote client, broadcast server, bench tools) buried third, after two long implementation-detail entries. For a first release, that's backwards - a reader's first look at this package shouldn't open on punctuation internals.
Regrouped by theme instead: on-device live transcription (including routing and the two-pass refine) opens it, then the remote client, the LAN broadcast server, runtime configuration/events/reset (#29), decoding off the UI isolate (#24) with its three incidental bug fixes folded in, Japanese punctuation (#15) with its "refine only, model not downloadable yet" caveats kept front and center rather than buried at the end, and bench/eval utilities. Added a "Known limitations" section at the end pulling together caveats that were previously scattered across bullets (no app-lifecycle handling, textTransform's scope, no diarization, unimplemented translation event, no device run for punctuation) so a reader evaluating the package for production doesn't have to reconstruct that list from prose.
No facts changed - every number, API name, and caveat is carried over from the existing text; this is a reorganization, not new content.
Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
* docs(hayamimi_core): reorganize the README as a pub.dev landing page
pub.dev renders this file from the package directory (not the repo root), so every relative link to a repo file resolved to a 404 there - and dartdoc's own link validator already flagged six of them as broken for the same reason (fixed here as a side effect; the standalone dartdoc's 11-warnings baseline drops to 5 from this alone, before the lib/ doc-reference fixes in the prior commit). Converted every relative lib/example link to an absolute github.com/oboroge0/hayamimi/blob/main/... URL.
Beyond the link fix, restructured for a pub.dev first-time reader rather than a repo browser who already has the source open: added a table of contents; grouped the embedding-relevant sections under one "Embedding guide" heading in the order a new integration actually needs them (initialize sherpa_onnx.initBindings() - previously undocumented at the README level even though the example does it and native_model_loader.dart explains why it's required - platform permissions, the two facades, runtime config, punctuation, threading, events); consolidated the model-file material into one "Model placement guide" with an explicit directory-layout table (which files in model/, vad/, sense_voice/, lid/, and where the punctuation files go) alongside the existing download/manual-placement instructions and a pointer to THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md for licensing; and replaced the punctuation-only platform table with a package-wide "Platform status" table built from docs/MOBILE.md and docs/IOS_VERIFY.md, stating plainly that Android has only ever been exercised on an emulator (host PC CPU, not a real device) while iOS has real iPhone 15 verification for bench/live-mic/routing but not remote mode or punctuation.
Existing section substance (threading model, event JSON shapes, package layout, measured numbers and their conditions) is carried over, not rewritten - no new numbers were introduced, and every existing measured number kept the conditions it was recorded under.
Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
* docs(hayamimi_core): scope THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md to this package
Both files had been copied from the desktop hayamimi pipeline's own notices and only added to, never trimmed - so a pub.dev reader auditing this Flutter package's licenses saw entries for Paraformer-zh, Parakeet TDT, Omnilingual, CAM++ speaker embedding, M2M-100/FuguMT translation (including the CC BY-SA 4.0 share-alike warning), and a Python dependencies table (ctranslate2, sentencepiece, fugashi, kiwipiepy, ...) - none of which this package uses. LICENSE's addendum specifically warned about FuguMT's CC BY-SA 4.0 terms, which don't apply here since this package never bundles or downloads that model.
Rewrote THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md to cover exactly what hayamimi_core uses: the four ASR/VAD models downloadProfile or manual placement can put on a phone (ReazonSpeech, Silero VAD, SenseVoice, whisper-tiny), the optional Japanese punctuation model, and the package's own six Dart dependencies (including onnxruntime, used transitively through sherpa_onnx and directly through this package's own dart:ffi bindings) with their actual licenses checked against each package's own LICENSE file in the pub cache - record's BSD-3-Clause text carries a mismatched "Copyright 2022 openapi4j authors" header (that package's own artifact, not something to fix here). Kept the vendored ONNX Runtime bindings section, the FLEURS test-fixture attribution, and the Mojicast credit, all unchanged since they're accurate as written. Reworded LICENSE's addendum to name the models this package actually places instead of the desktop-only translation model.
Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
* docs: point mobile/ and MOBILE.md at the hayamimi_core package guide
mobile/README.md: noted hayamimi_core is now published on pub.dev, so a third-party app can depend on it directly instead of copying this repo's path/git dependency form.
docs/MOBILE.md: this file is an investigation log (model sizing, quantization, on-device measurements) that a reader searching for "mobile" + "hayamimi" is likely to land on, but it never pointed anywhere for the actual embedding guide - added one line at the top to mobile/hayamimi_core/README.md, which is where issue #16's pub.dev release work landed the model-placement and platform-status reference these measurements now feed into.
Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
* live: decode each segment with the second of audio before it
Silero VAD reports a speech onset slightly after the speaker actually started, so the samples it hands over can begin partway into the first word and the recognizer transcribes that word wrong. On the Android emulator run of this package, `資料は昨日送りました` came back as `昨日は昨日送りました` and `あしたの会議は十時からです` lost its `あしたの` outright -- both utterance-initial, both clipped by the onset.
The desktop pipeline has never had that problem, because it does not decode the VAD's samples as-is: `AudioHistory` (scripts/realtime_transcribe.py) keeps a rolling buffer of recent audio and prepends up to PREROLL_S = 1.0 seconds of it to every segment, clamped so it never reaches back into the previous one. tests/test_asr_segment.py pins that on the same fixture that regressed here. This is that, in Dart, on the caller's isolate.
`PrerollHistory` (lib/live/preroll.dart) is the whole mechanism and is pure Dart, so it is unit tested directly: frames in, bounded, and a segment out with its run-up attached -- never past what the buffer still holds, never past where the last segment ended. A session pushes every frame it feeds the VAD into one of these and asks for the extended segment when the VAD finalizes one.
Two pieces of plumbing this needed. `LiveVad.takeSegment` now returns a `LiveSpeechSegment` (samples plus the segment's start position) rather than bare samples, because the samples alone do not say where "just before" is; and `LiveTranscriber` tracks how much audio it had fed when the current VAD instance was installed, so a mid-session sensitivity swap -- which gives it a VAD counting from zero again -- does not shift every position after it.
For a caller: a final now covers the pre-roll as well as the speech, so `audioSeconds` grows by up to a second and the refine ("清書") buffer stores the same extended audio the desktop's history does. The new `prerollSeconds` knob (constructor plus runtime setter on both `LiveTranscriber` and `HayamimiLive`) tunes it, and is the one pacing knob where 0 is a valid value: it means "decode exactly what the VAD delimited".
Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
* live: split segments on the pauses the desktop splits on
`VadSensitivity` shipped with sherpa-onnx's own stock values, and the class doc said so as if that were the safe choice. The Android emulator run of this package showed what it costs. On a three-sentence Japanese recording whose inter-sentence pauses fall just under half a second, the stock 0.5 s silence default merged all three sentences into a single 6.13 s segment; handed that segment, this repo's ja recognizer returned only the last sentence. Two sentences vanished, with nothing in the output to say so -- a wrong caption rather than a rough one.
The desktop pipeline this package is the mobile port of does not use the stock values. It runs --min-silence 0.35 and --max-speech 12.0 (scripts/realtime_transcribe.py), and its own comment records that 0.35 s measured no worse for accuracy than 0.5 s on real broadcast Japanese while finalizing a segment 150 ms sooner. Re-running the same audio through this package at 0.35 s split it into three segments and all three sentences came out. So the defaults here are now the desktop's: minSilenceSeconds 0.35, maxSpeechSeconds 12.0. threshold and minSpeechSeconds are unchanged; the desktop leaves those alone too.
The maxSpeechSeconds doc also stops promising something that did not hold. It called itself a hard cap that force-closes a segment "even mid-speech", but the same run emitted a 6.134 s segment from a session configured with 5.0 s. sherpa-onnx's max_speech_duration influences when the VAD closes a segment; it does not bound what the VAD can hand over, and the doc now says that, so nobody sizes a buffer or a timeout on the old promise.
For a caller who passes no vadSensitivity: segments now finalize on shorter pauses, so a transcript has more lines, each shorter, and each decoded from audio the recognizer can actually handle. Passing VadSensitivity(minSilenceSeconds: 0.5, maxSpeechSeconds: 5.0) restores the previous behavior exactly.
Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
* live: end a debug wav stream with the refine it promises
`startDebugWavStream` says it emits "the same events a live mic session would", and it is the package's answer to an emulator having no usable microphone -- the README points at it as the way to see punctuated refine output. With default settings it could not produce a refine at all. Auto refine is off by default, so nothing fired during the stream; and the method tears the session down in its own `finally`, so by the time its future completes `refineNow()` has no worker left to ask and silently returns having done nothing. The Android emulator run measured exactly that: a `refineNow()` after the await returned in 0 ms with an empty buffer.
Two things were also true and undocumented: setting `autoRefineEnabled` before the call does work (the debug path's session reset starts the timer when the flag is already set), and `refineNow()` works if called from another async context while the stream is still running.
So: after the last segment is flushed and its decode has drained, the stream now runs one refine over what those finals buffered -- if they add up to at least half a second, the same floor the refine payload itself applies -- and awaits it before teardown. The `autoRefineEnabled` setter also starts its timer for a debug stream, not only a microphone session, so turning auto refine on mid-stream works the way it reads. Both are documented on `LiveTranscriber.startDebugWavStream` and `HayamimiLive.startDebugWavStream`, including that the session is gone before the future completes, which is why a caller cannot ask for a refine afterwards.
One bug fixed alongside: the debug path never cancelled its auto-refine timer, since only `stop()` does that and `stop()` only ends a microphone session. Before this change nothing started that timer on this path in practice; now that both paths can, the `finally` cancels it, so a finished stream does not leave a timer ticking against a torn-down session for the life of the object.
For a caller, one awaited `startDebugWavStream` call is now enough to see a punctuated refine on a device with no microphone -- which is what the method existed for.
Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
* docs: record what the Android emulator run verified, and what it changed
The decode worker (#24) and the Dart punctuation port (#15) had both been built without ever running on Android, and the docs said so. They have now run there, on an x86_64 emulator, and the same session turned up two ways the mobile port produced worse text than the desktop pipeline on the same recording -- which is what the VAD-default and pre-roll changes in this branch came from. This writes all of that down.
docs/MOBILE.md gets the full account: the setup, why each of the two targets was worth doubting on Android in the first place, what the run showed (the worker spawning and loading models inside itself, torn down and rebuilt three times in one process; exactly one libonnxruntime.so in the APK, ONNX Runtime 1.27.1 through it, ja refines punctuated at the same sentence ends as the Python reference), the timings with their conditions, the two segmentation findings and what this branch did about them, and the truncation that is the recogniser model's own property rather than anything this package can fix.
The package README says the same, shorter, where a reader of the package will look: the Android rows of both platform-status tables, a timing table labelled for what it is, the pre-roll row in the pacing-knob table, the reason the VAD defaults are the desktop's, and a known-limitation section for the long-group refine.
Two things are stated the same way everywhere, because both are easy to misread. Nothing here is a phone measurement -- an emulator's CPU is the host desktop's under virtualization, and ONNX Runtime has no float16 compute path on x86, so the punctuation timings in particular do not transfer. And punctuation was never timed on its own: a refine's latency_ms covers the re-decode and restore() together, so the 26-33 ms per ~10 characters quoted for it is a refine minus the final over the same samples, an inference from two timers rather than a measurement.
Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
* live: punctuate Japanese finals, so a refine's fallback keeps its marks
A refine ("清書") does not always emit its own text. When the merged re-decode comes back much shorter than the fast finals it is replacing, `isRefineTextTooShort` rejects it and the caller emits those finals joined instead. Those finals were never punctuated, so the refine went out raw -- losing the marks in exactly the case the guard exists to protect. The Android emulator run hit this on package defaults: three good finals, a re-decode holding only the last sentence, and `refine punctuated=false text=東京の天気は晴れです あしたの会議は十時からです 資料は昨日送りました`. With `defaultAutoRefineSilenceSeconds` at 4.0 a microphone session groups several sentences per refine, so on this recognizer that was the normal outcome, not a corner case.
The worker now punctuates `finalSegment` results under the same condition it punctuates refines -- routed `lang == 'ja'`, or a plain session flagged Japanese -- so the joined fast text is already punctuated and the fallback has something punctuated to fall back to. That is what the desktop pipeline relies on: `RoutedASR.transcribe` punctuates its ja finals, so `realtime_transcribe.py`'s identical fallback yields punctuated text. Drafts stay unpunctuated; they cover part of a sentence still being spoken and are re-decoded about once a second.
`RefineSegment` and `RefineRequestPayload` carry whether their text is punctuated, so the fallback reports `punctuated: true` only when every final in the group was; the shrink comparison now strips the restored marks off both sides, since either can have them. `JaPunctuation` gains `applyToFinals` (default true) for a caller who wants the fast line left exactly as the recognizer produced it and will take the old fallback behaviour with it.
Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
* events: say on a final line whether it was punctuated
A finalized line can now carry 、 and 。 (the previous commit), and a consumer had no way to tell one that does from one the recognizer wrote bare -- `punctuated` existed on `RefineSubtitleEvent` but not on `FinalSubtitleEvent`, so the same fact was reportable for one pass and not the other.
`FinalSubtitleEvent` gains `punctuated` (wire key `"punctuated"`, default false; every key that was already there still is), `HayamimiLive` forwards `LiveTranscriptEntry.punctuated` onto it, and `RemoteFinalEvent` parses the key when a server sends it. No server sends it today -- `subtitle_server.py` has no such key on `final` frames -- so a remote session reports false; the field is there so a consumer reads the same field from the on-device and remote paths rather than one that only some producers have.
Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
* docs: record why the fast line is punctuated, and what the second emulator run measured
The README described punctuation as a refine-only feature and explained the fallback as a case where the marks are simply lost. Both are now wrong, and the reason they changed is worth writing down rather than paraphrasing: the second Android emulator run showed the closing refine coming out `punctuated=false` on package defaults, over three sentences the fast path had recognized correctly.
README: the punctuation section says refines and finals (and why drafts are excluded), a new "Why the fast line is punctuated too" subsection carries the emulator line, the mechanism, the desktop comparison and the `applyToFinals` switch with its measured cost, the events table's `final` row gains `punctuated`, and the emulator timing table is replaced with the second run's numbers (n=10 model loads, per-segment final medians, warm and first-in- process refines), labelled as the second run. Both emulator runs predate punctuated finals, so the platform-status row says the fast line's punctuation has been seen only in this package's tests.
CHANGELOG: the punctuation entry describes what ships, and a new entry records the third defect and the fix, including that it is unverified on a device.
docs/MOBILE.md: a run-2 section — the run 1 / run 2 / desktop text and `audio_s` comparison, the two controls (`prerollSeconds: 0` reproduces run 1 exactly; the old VAD values reproduce its merged segment), the closing refine firing on true defaults, the timings, and the third defect with its mechanism and the change this branch makes for it.
Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
* live: join a punctuated fallback's finals without spaces
The Android emulator's third run found that a refine's fallback text -- combineSegmentFastText, joining the buffered group's fast finals when the merged re-decode is rejected as too short -- still used the same join(' ') that was right when finals were unpunctuated but wrong now that they carry marks: every sentence already ends in 。, so a following space is a second, redundant separator and not how Japanese is set. The desktop's own refine output for the same fixture has none.
combineSegmentFastText now joins with '' when isCombinedFastTextPunctuated says every contributing segment was punctuated, and keeps ' ' otherwise, so an unpunctuated fallback still has a separator. The fp16 punctuation model's first restore() in a process costs ~300 ms more than every later one. entry.title: Punctuation (#15 phase 1, Dart): PunctuatorJa port over sherpa's ONNX…
entry.content:
Punctuation (#15 phase 1, Dart): PunctuatorJa port over sherpa's ONNX Runtime via dart:ffi, host parity test (#50)

* eval: record the Python punctuation output as a Dart parity fixture

A Dart port of scripts/punct_ja.py is only trustworthy if it is pinned to
the reference implementation on real sentences, not on hand-written
examples that both sides were written to satisfy.

scripts/make_punct_fixture.py takes 40 Japanese sentences from the FLEURS
ja benchmark set, strips their punctuation to make ASR-like input, and
records for each one the token ids PunctuatorJa feeds the model and the
string its restore() returns with the fp16 model loaded. It adds 11
synthetic cases for what FLEURS ja does not contain: question endings
(FLEURS ja is news prose and holds no questions at all), empty and
punctuation-only input, half-width kana, and input past the 500-character
cut.

Recording the token ids separately from the output is what lets the Dart
side check tokenization without the 182 MB model, so half the parity
survives on a machine that does not have it.

The script also re-checks the assumption the Dart tokenizer rests on --
that MeCab's only observable effect here is dropping whitespace -- and
refuses to write the fixture if the two ever disagree. Right now they
agree on all 102 texts checked.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(mobile): restore Japanese punctuation in hayamimi_core

The desktop pipeline runs its refine ("清書") text through
scripts/punct_ja.py before anything sees it, so desktop captions read as
sentences. hayamimi_core had no equivalent, so its refine output arrived
as an unbroken run of characters -- same words, no 、 and no 。.

PunctuatorJa.restore(String) is a Dart port of that script: the same
character-level BERT model, the same 0.5 thresholds, the same rule-based
？ pass. Phase 1 of #15 -- this adds the component, it does not yet wire
it into HayamimiLive.

lib/punct/ splits along one line: everything except two files is plain
Dart, unit-testable without a model. punct_ja_tokenizer.dart turns text
into the model's character tokens; punct_ja_text.dart decides where a
mark goes. punct_ort_session.dart and ort_library.dart are the only FFI.

Reaching ONNX Runtime is the part with a decision in it. Adding the
onnxruntime or flutter_onnxruntime package would put a second
libonnxruntime.so in the app, and two copies in one Android process is a
known crash (k2-fsa/sherpa-onnx#3261). So this ships no runtime: it looks
up OrtGetApiBase in the library sherpa_onnx has already loaded and calls
the C API through dart:ffi. ONNX Runtime's function table only grows at
the end across releases, so asking for API version 11 keeps the bindings
valid as sherpa_onnx bumps what it bundles. The session is built from the
model's file path, never from bytes, so 182 MB does not pass through the
Dart heap; every native object is freed explicitly.

Android is expected to work but was not run on a device. iOS is refused
by default with an explanatory exception: sherpa_onnx links ONNX Runtime
as an xcframework and it is unconfirmed that OrtGetApiBase stays exported
from the app binary, so guessing would be worse than saying so.

Two dependencies. unorm_dart supplies NFKC, a Unicode normalization
dart:core has no equivalent of and the tokenizer needs to match Python.
ffi supplies native allocation. MeCab, the other half of the reference
tokenizer, is not replaced at all: the pipeline splits every morpheme
back into single characters a line later, so MeCab's only observable
effect is dropping whitespace, and the Dart tokenizer does that directly.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(mobile): pin the Dart punctuation port to the Python reference

Unit tests say each rule behaves as written; they cannot say the rules
add up to the same text scripts/punct_ja.py produces. So the load-bearing
test replays the recorded fixture end to end -- 40 FLEURS ja sentences
plus 11 edge cases through the fp16 model -- and asserts the Dart output
equals the Python output character for character. It passes on all 51.

Neither the 182 MB model nor an ONNX Runtime library is in the
repository, so the test skips with a reason naming whichever is missing
instead of failing, and a checkout without them stays green. On Windows
it borrows the onnxruntime.dll that sherpa_onnx_windows ships, resolved
through .dart_tool/package_config.json rather than hardcoded, so a
version bump does not break it; elsewhere HAYAMIMI_ORT_LIBRARY points at
one.

punct_ja_fixture_tokens_test.dart checks the same fixture's token ids and
needs only the 28 KB vocab.txt, so the tokenizer -- the piece most likely
to drift, since it replaces MeCab and unicodedata with hand-written rules
-- stays covered without the model.

The parity test also prints its mean restore() latency, labelled as this
Windows x86 host: 66-71 ms across runs. That number says nothing about a
phone and the message says so, because ONNX Runtime's CPU provider has no
float16 path on x86 and casts every operator's tensors to float32 and
back.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs: document the Dart punctuation port, and what it does not do yet

Someone picking up hayamimi_core needs to know three things about the new
PunctuatorJa that the code alone does not say: why the mobile package was
missing punctuation at all, why the ONNX Runtime access looks so
roundabout, and which platforms this has actually been run on.

The README gains a section covering all three. The platform table states
plainly that only the Windows host is verified, that Android is expected
to work but was never run on a device, and that iOS is refused by default
because sherpa_onnx's xcframework may not export OrtGetApiBase. It also
records what the parity test measured and, more importantly, why that
number does not transfer to a phone.

It also says what is still missing: the restorer is not wired into
HayamimiLive, and the model file is not downloadable -- 181.8 MB with no
hosting decision made.

THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES gains the attribution the code owes: the trimmed ONNX
Runtime bindings derived from gtbluesky/onnxruntime_flutter (MIT, itself
generated from Microsoft's MIT-licensed header), unorm_dart (MIT) and ffi
(BSD-3-Clause), and the fixture's FLEURS sentences (CC BY 4.0).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs: stop attributing the Dart-vs-Python latency gap to the runtime build

The README compared the Dart port's 66-71 ms mean restore() with the
Python reference's 366.3 ms on the same host and stated the gap was "between
two ONNX Runtime builds, not between the two implementations". That was a
guess: the two timings differ in ONNX Runtime build (1.27.1 vs 1.29.0),
intra-op thread count (2 vs 4) and in what the timed call includes (the
Python number contains MeCab tokenization), and nobody isolated any of
those. Keep the measurement, drop the attribution, and say plainly that the
cause was not investigated.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Decode off the UI isolate (#24): persistent decode worker, explicit q…
entry.content:
Decode off the UI isolate (#24): persistent decode worker, explicit queue policy, testable VAD seam (#49)

* live: a decode worker isolate that owns the session's recognizers

Every sherpa-onnx call is synchronous FFI: it runs to completion on the
isolate that makes it, and a Dart isolate is single-threaded, so nothing
else on it happens meanwhile. Model loading already moved off the caller's
isolate for that reason; decoding did not, so a host app stopped painting
for the length of every utterance's decode, and for much longer during a
refine pass over a whole buffered group.

This adds the machinery for moving it, without wiring it up yet:

- decode_protocol.dart: the request/result message types and their wire
  encoding. Audio travels as TransferableTypedData, which moves a refine
  pass's buffer through external memory rather than copying it into the
  receiving isolate's collected heap.
- decode_scheduler.dart: the queue policy, as a pure state machine. Being
  synchronous used to *be* the mutual exclusion, so each kind of request
  now needs an explicit rule -- finals queue, drafts are dropped, refines
  coalesce.
- decode_worker.dart: the worker isolate itself, and the handle it is
  driven through. It builds its own recognizers, because the objects never
  leave it and there is no pointer handoff to justify, and it serves one
  request at a time, which is the same exclusion the old code got for free.
- decode_session.dart: the caller's-isolate half -- request ids, dispatch,
  staleness, and the futures refineNow/resetSession hand out.

RoutedRecognizerSet.build gains loadOffIsolate so the worker can build its
three models in place instead of spawning a nested isolate per model; it
defaults to today's behaviour for every other caller.

Nothing calls any of this yet, so nothing changes for a caller.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* live: send every decode to the worker instead of running it inline

LiveTranscriber decoded each VAD segment, each draft and each refine pass
with a synchronous FFI call on whichever isolate drove the mic stream --
the host app's UI isolate. The app stopped painting for the length of each
one. This routes all of them through the decode worker added in the
previous commit, so the caller's isolate keeps only mic capture, one Silero
VAD acceptWaveform per 32 ms frame, and event dispatch.

The parts that only worked because decoding was synchronous had to be
rebuilt around a queue:

- _busy is no longer a flag set around a call; it is the decode queue's own
  state, so `decoding` now emits one true/false pair per burst rather than
  one per decode. isDraftDue and shouldSwapVadNow read the same thing and
  keep their meaning.
- Drafts are stamped with a segment id that is bumped whenever a segment
  opens or closes, so a draft answered after its segment already produced a
  final is discarded instead of overwriting it.
- refineNow's future now completes when its result has been emitted, and it
  claims the buffered audio at dispatch rather than at the call, so a
  segment still decoding when the user taps the refine button joins that
  group instead of the next one.
- resetSession no longer polls a busy flag; the clear is queued behind
  whatever the worker already has and completes on the worker's ack.
- stop() waits (bounded) for the queue to drain before shutting the worker
  down, so the segment its VAD flush produces still reaches `entries` --
  which used to happen for free.

A worker that dies mid-session is handled like a revoked microphone: a
LiveTranscriberException on `errors`, capture torn down, the object left
restartable. A build failure inside the worker comes back out of start() as
the same LiveTranscriberException text callers saw before, with the worker
already cleaned up. Late replies from a stopped session are ignored via the
existing session-generation counter.

Every public signature, stream and event is unchanged; currentLang is now a
mirror updated from worker replies. startDebugWavStream goes through the
same path, so an emulator run exercises the worker too;
runDebugWavRefineTest still decodes in place and now says so.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test: cover the decode protocol, the queue policy, and the worker lifecycle

The decode path was untested because it needed the sherpa-onnx native
libraries and a real microphone, neither of which a flutter test run has.
Splitting the work into a message protocol, a pure queue policy, and a
caller's-isolate coordinator driven through an injectable worker interface
means most of it no longer does.

- decode_protocol_test.dart: every request and result round-trips its
  fields, including a sample view sent from the middle of a buffer, which
  is what capDraftWindow hands over.
- decode_scheduler_test.dart: finals queue in order, drafts are dropped
  while anything is outstanding, refines fold into a queued one but not
  into one already sent, and clear returns the in-flight request first.
- decode_session_test.dart: a whole session against a scripted stand-in
  worker -- finals answered in order with their own audio, a stale draft
  discarded, a refine claiming its buffer at dispatch, a reset landing
  behind the work it must not race, a decode failing without stopping the
  session, and a worker dying mid-session.
- live_transcriber_decode_test.dart: what start() hands the worker, that a
  build failure comes back as the same LiveTranscriberException text, and
  that a failure after the worker is up still shuts it down.
- isolate_decode_worker_test.dart: the real spawn/error/exit plumbing, as
  far as a test VM that cannot load the native library can go.

What is still only verifiable on a device: whether a decode produces the
right text, and what any of this does to frame timing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs: describe what runs where now that decoding is off the caller's isolate

The README's "Threading / known limitations" section told readers that
per-segment decode ran on their isolate and pointed at the issue tracker
for a fix. That is no longer true, and a package about to be published
should not ship a section describing the shape of a problem it has since
moved.

The section now says which isolate each piece of work runs on, spells out
the queue rules a caller can observe (finals in order, drafts dropped and
discarded, refines coalesced, `decoding` once per burst), and states two
things plainly rather than implying otherwise: decode latency is unchanged,
because the work moved rather than shrank, and no on-device frame-timing
measurement was taken for this change. It also documents what happens when
the worker dies, why a shutdown that times out frees nothing, and that
runDebugWavRefineTest still decodes in place.

CHANGELOG gains the same under 0.1.0, and the resetSession, source-layout
and testing sections are corrected to match.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* live: say why a routed decode worker refused to build

decodeWorkerMain dereferenced senseVoiceModelDir/lidModelDir with `!`.
LiveTranscriber checks both before spawning anything, so the path is
unreachable from the facade -- but decodeWorkerMain is exported, and
someone driving it directly would have got a build failure reading "Null
check operator used on a null value" instead of a sentence naming the two
missing arguments. Now it names them.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* live: stop a worker build failure racing the exit port into a StateError

IsolateDecodeWorker settles its `_ready` completer from two directions: the
`build_failed` frame the worker sends, and the error/exit ports reporting
that it is gone. Those race, and a failing worker triggers both -- it sends
the frame and then exits. The death path guarded against completing twice;
the frame path did not, so if the exit landed first, `_ready.completeError`
ran on an already-completed completer. That throws a StateError inside a
port listener, where no caller can catch it: an unhandled async error
instead of the DecodeWorkerException start() was about to throw.

Both directions now go through the same guarded helpers, with the reason
written down next to them.

The isolate test now waits for both messages to land before finishing, so
the ordering that does occur is covered; flutter_test fails on an unhandled
async error, which is what this would produce. Forcing the reverse
interleaving would need a seam for Isolate.spawn itself, which is more
machinery than this guard is worth.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* live: put a seam in front of the VAD, so a running session is testable

The decode worker got an interface so tests could stand in for it, but that
was only one of the two FFI edges a session has. LiveTranscriber reaches
isRunning == true only after it has loaded a Silero VAD, which no
flutter test run can do, so everything a *live* session does -- segments
becoming transcript lines in order, drafts being skipped and then discarded,
a worker dying with the microphone open, a reply landing after stop() --
was reachable only on a device, and this branch had reasoned about all of
it rather than tested it.

live_vad.dart adds the missing half: a LiveVad interface of the six calls
LiveTranscriber actually makes (feed a frame, is speech in progress, take a
finished segment, flush, free, frame size), a LiveVadFactory, and
SileroLiveVad wrapping sherpa-onnx exactly as before. The production path
is unchanged -- buildSileroLiveVad is the constructor default and still
loads off-isolate through native_model_loader.dart; the config building
that lived in LiveTranscriber moved next to the implementation that uses
it.

Two things follow from the seam:

- isSegmentWorthDecoding now takes the samples rather than a
  sherpa_onnx.SpeechSegment. LiveTranscriber no longer sees that type at
  all, and the helper (and its test) are now free of the FFI-backed package
  entirely.
- startDebugWavStream reads its wav with this package's own pure-Dart
  parser instead of sherpa-onnx's readWave. Same accepted format -- both
  handle 16-bit PCM only -- but it keeps the streaming debug path free of
  FFI, so a test can push a file through the whole VAD/draft/final/refine
  pipeline. Channel count is now checked explicitly, where readWave would
  have failed less clearly.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test: drive a whole live session, microphone to transcript line

With both FFI edges behind seams, a LiveTranscriber can now reach
isRunning == true in a plain flutter test run, so the behaviour this branch
changed is checked rather than argued for. Fifteen tests against a fake
recorder, a scripted fake VAD and a fake decode worker:

- two segments become two lines, in order, with text, lang, switched,
  audioSeconds and latencyMs all populated, the refine buffer filled, and
  one busy transition for the burst rather than one per decode;
- an empty result buffers nothing, and a segment under the minimum duration
  never reaches the worker at all;
- a draft goes out mid-utterance; none is even *queued* while a final is
  outstanding (checked by letting the final finish and watching nothing
  follow it out); one whose segment closed while it was decoding is
  discarded, and the final that superseded it is emitted instead;
- two refineNow calls yield one pass, covering the segment that was still
  decoding when the caller asked;
- resetSession lands behind that segment, then clears and reports;
- a worker dying stops the session, reports exactly once, frees the VAD, and
  leaves the object restartable; a single failed decode reports without
  stopping anything;
- stop() emits the segment its VAD flush produces before returning, and a
  reply arriving after it emits nothing;
- startDebugWavStream feeds a real wav file through and flushes its last
  segment, and rejects one at the wrong sample rate without leaving a worker
  or a VAD behind.

Each of these was mutation-checked: breaking the staleness comparison, both
draft-skip guards, the worker-death teardown, or stop()'s drain makes the
corresponding test fail. One thing is deliberately not claimed here --
that a second refineNow returns the *same* future -- because refineNow is an
async wrapper and necessarily hands out a fresh one; that half of coalescing
is asserted on DecodeSession, and the comment says so.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs: record the VAD seam and what a live session's tests now cover

The README's source-layout and testing sections were written when the
decode worker was the only thing a test could stand in for, so they
described coverage that has since grown: a whole live session is now driven
end to end, and the FFI itself is what is left untested. The CHANGELOG's
list of new building blocks likewise predates live_vad.dart, and did not
mention two changes a caller could notice -- isSegmentWorthDecoding's
signature, and startDebugWavStream reading its wav in Dart.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
